## Summary

A build-vs-buy take on agentic code review: for the **best cost/quality balance, skip the SaaS codex/claude reviewer products**. Instead, **create your own agent triggered by GitHub webhooks on PR-raised/updated events**, and **give it company and architecture context** (tweet truncates mid-way through what context to give).

## Why it matters

- **The counter-position to the SaaS case.** The quoted tweet (@bcherny, presumably Anthropic-adjacent) is the strongest public endorsement of the managed product; this tweet is the direct rebuttal from the same timeline. Useful as the anchor of a pro/con pair on agentic review tooling.
- **"Company and architecture context" is the load-bearing claim.** That's the actual argument: a generic reviewer pays for multi-tenant convenience with context-blindness, while a self-hosted webhook agent can be fed the repo's own conventions, architecture docs, and review priors — the same context-engineering bet as [[2026-10-13-dearlordylord-specs-as-state-machine]] (ground the agent in *your* real artifacts, not generic priors).
- **Build-vs-buy economics, echoing a recurring theme.** Same shape as [[2026-10-07-paulsanglef-4x-commits-devsetup-ci]]: own your dev loop's agent layer because the marginal cost is low (webhook + prompt + context files) and the fit to your codebase is the whole value. Craig's framing is explicitly **cost-quality balance**, not maximal quality.
- **Skepticism gates:** single tweet, truncated mid-argument (the numbered recipe is incomplete — we don't see what "any key…" context items are); 37 replies unread; no cost numbers, no quality comparison, no mention of maintenance burden (self-hosted review agents rot: webhook infra, model drift, prompt upkeep). The SaaS side of the trade (zero setup, updates included) is argued only by the quoted tweet, not evaluated.
